newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN chief says troops in Macedonia can be reduced.
newsitem.headline: UN chief says troops in Macedonia can be reduced.

text.p: The United Nations said on Thursday its troop reduction for Macedonia could now go ahead because the turmoil in neighboring Albania had subsided.

In a report to the Security Council, Secretary-General Kofi Annan said it was possible to reduce the force of 1,050 by 300 soldiers, starting in October, as requested by the Council but suspended because of the violence in Albania.
The Macedonia operation includes nearly 500 United States troops, 350 soldiers from Finland and small contigents from Indonesia, Denmark, Norway and Sweden.
The U.N. Preventive Deployment Force, known as UNPREDP, was originally deployed to prevent conflicts elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia from spilling over into Macedonia, a former Yugoslav republic.

The Security Council last November called for a phased reduction of 300 soldiers to be completed by April 30. But on April 9 the council suspended the drawdown because of unrest in Albania. The mandate for UNPREDEP expires at the end of November but is expected to be renewed.
Annan, in his report, said the United Nations now had to analyze what kind of an operation was needed for Macedonia for te rest of the year and after the troops eventually leave.

"Internally economic and social problems continue to pose a significant threat to the country's integration and long-term stabiity and further exacerbate inter-ethnic tensions," he said, alluding to divisions involving the country's large Albanian minority.
"These internal problems give rise to the question of whether the current mandate of UNPREDEP is relevant to the present situation (and) whether it can be implemented with fewer resources," he said.
He said a two-month phased reduction of 300 troops would begin on October 1 "bearing in mind the conditions prevailing over that time in the region."
In the meantime, he said he was exploring "practical options for flexible redployment of the force" and studying the what kind of international presense was needed for the future.

The report also said that relations had improved considerably with Yugoslavia but that no agreement had been reached on demarcating their common border. Work, he said, had "far fallen short of the expectations and the public statement of intent of the two parties."
